import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Maximality of $k = 43$ with restricted digit counts in bases $3 \le b < k$

Numbers $k$ such that the base $b$ expansion of $k$ for each
$b = 3..k-1$ never contains more than two distinct digits.

The sequence Numbers $k$ such that the base $b$ expansion of $k$ for each
$b = 3..k-1$ never contains more than two distinct digits.

*References:*
- [A306424](https://oeis.org/A306424)
- [arxiv/2605.22763](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22763) *Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search* by George Tsoukalas et al.
-/

namespace OeisA306424


open List Finset Nat

/--
Numbers $k$ such that the base $b$ expansion of $k$ for each
$b = 3..k-1$ never contains more than two distinct digits.
-/
def Condition (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  -- The bases $b$ range over $3 \le b \le k-1$, expressed as $3 \le b$ and $b < k$.
  ∀ b : ℕ, 3 ≤ b ∧ b < k → ((Nat.digits b k).toFinset.card) ≤ 2

/--
The $n$-th number $k$ such that the base $b$ expansion of $k$ for each
$b = 3..k-1$ never contains more than two distinct digits.
-/
noncomputable def a (n : ℕ) : ℕ := n.nth Condition


@[category test, AMS 11]
lemma a_1 : a 1 = 1 := by sorry

@[category test, AMS 11]
lemma a_2 : a 2 = 2 := by sorry

@[category test, AMS 11]
lemma a_3 : a 3 = 3 := by sorry

@[category test, AMS 11]
lemma a_4 : a 4 = 4 := by sorry

@[category test, AMS 11]
lemma a_5 : a 5 = 5 := by sorry


/--
Conjecture: The sequence is finite, with 43 being the last term.

A formal proof has been found with the methods described in
[arxiv/2605.22763](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22763).
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using formal_conjectures at
"https://github.com/mo271/formal-conjectures/blob/a32396489dcb8f86c3549b93aa358ac6a10a3a1f/FormalConjectures/OEIS/306424.wip.lean#L276"]
theorem forty_three_is_max : Condition 43 ∧ ∀ k : ℕ, 43 < k → ¬Condition k := by
    sorry

end OeisA306424

reformulations.difference: OEIS enumerates positive qualifying numbers starting at index 1, whereas Lean uses the zero-indexed Nat.nth on Condition, which also admits 0.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Condition 0 holds vacuously, and 0 is the unique extra smallest element. In scratch.lean I proved, for every n > 0, a n = Nat.nth (fun k => 0 < k ∧ Condition k) (n - 1). Thus the inclusion of zero exactly compensates for Nat.nth's zero-based indexing. I also independently proved agreement with every b-file entry at indices 1 through 23. Values at index 0 and beyond the finite sequence are harmless totalizations outside OEIS's index domain.

reformulations.difference: The source says the sequence is finite with last term 43; Lean instead asserts Condition 43 and the failure of Condition for every larger natural number, without a separate finiteness assertion.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For S = {k : ℕ | 0 < k ∧ Condition k}, the Lean statement implies S is bounded above by 43 and contains 43. Hence S is finite and IsGreatest S 43. Conversely, IsGreatest S 43 supplies Condition 43 and excludes every k > 43, since such k are positive. I proved the exact equivalence with S.Finite ∧ IsGreatest S 43 in scratch.lean.

review.notes: All eight declarations were checked. Nat.digits has the correct canonical digit semantics; its little-endian order does not affect toFinset.card, and bases 0, 1, and 2 are excluded. Independent kernel proofs verified the five test declarations and all 23 OEIS terms. Evaluation for k < 1000 returned precisely zero plus the OEIS list. The current OEIS entry records the conjecture as proved, matching research solved. The exact cited proof has the same mathematical statement and contains no sorry or custom axioms. Its old tactic code required four helper-proof updates for the current toolchain; the resulting /workspace/review/cited-proof-ported.lean verified the repository statement using only propext, Classical.choice, and Quot.sound. No repository files were edited.
